◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Everything in multivariable calculus lives in 3D (or higher). Vectors are the language for position, direction, force, and velocity — and the dot product is the tool that measures angles and projections, which reappears in the gradient, work integrals, and least squares.

Vectors and length

A vector v = ⟨a, b, c⟩ has length (magnitude) |v| = √(a² + b² + c²). A unit vector in the direction of v is v/|v|.

Dot product
For a = ⟨a₁,a₂,a₃⟩ and b = ⟨b₁,b₂,b₃⟩, the dot product is a·b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃ — a single number (scalar). Geometrically, a·b = |a||b|cos θ, where θ is the angle between them.
WORKED EXAMPLE — angle between vectors

Find the angle between a = ⟨1, 2, 2⟩ and b = ⟨3, 0, 4⟩.

a·b = (1)(3) + (2)(0) + (2)(4) = 11. |a| = √(1+4+4) = 3, |b| = √(9+0+16) = 5.

cos θ = 11/(3·5) = 11/15 ≈ 0.733, so θ = cos⁻¹(0.733) ≈ 42.8°.

Orthogonality: two nonzero vectors are perpendicular exactly when a·b = 0 (because cos 90° = 0). The scalar projection of b onto a is (a·b)/|a|.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

The dot product returns a scalar, not a vector. If you get a vector, you used the cross product by mistake.

📊 FIGURE — The dot product and the projection
Drop a perpendicular from b onto the line of a: the shadow has length |b| cos θ, and u · v = |u||v| cos θ packages that geometry. Positive dot product = pointing broadly the same way; zero = perpendicular; negative = opposing.
"}, "CALC3/ch1/s2": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The cross product produces a vector perpendicular to two given vectors — exactly what you need to find the normal to a plane, the area of a parallelogram, and torque. It's the geometric counterpart to the dot product.

Cross product
a × b = ⟨a₂b₃ − a₃b₂, a₃b₁ − a₁b₃, a₁b₂ − a₂b₁⟩. It is a vector, perpendicular to both a and b (right-hand rule). Its length |a × b| = |a||b|sin θ equals the area of the parallelogram they span.
WORKED EXAMPLE — cross product and normal vector

Compute ⟨1, 0, 2⟩ × ⟨-1, 3, 1⟩.

i-component: (0)(1) − (2)(3) = −6. j-component: (2)(−1) − (1)(1) = −3, but the j term is subtracted, giving −[(1)(1) − (2)(−1)] = −(1 + 2) = −3. k-component: (1)(3) − (0)(−1) = 3.

Result: ⟨−6, −3, 3⟩. Check perpendicularity: ⟨−6,−3,3⟩·⟨1,0,2⟩ = −6 + 0 + 6 = 0 ✓.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

The cross product is not commutative: a × b = −(b × a). And a × a = 0 (a vector is parallel to itself, sin 0 = 0).

📊 FIGURE — The cross product and its parallelogram
u × v stands perpendicular to the plane of u and v (right-hand rule: fingers sweep u into v, thumb gives the direction). Its LENGTH equals the parallelogram’s area, |u||v|sin θ — which is why parallel vectors cross to zero.
📊 FIGURE — what the cross product does
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The basis cycle, and what reversing costs

The standard basis multiplies in a cycle — i → j → k → i:

i × j = k    j × k = i    k × i = j

Go backwards round the cycle and every result is negated: j × i = −k, k × j = −i, i × k = −j.

That is anticommutativity: a × b = −(b × a), which follows from the right-hand rule — reversing the order reverses which way your thumb points. Contrast the dot product, which is fully commutative.

One consequence worth remembering: a × a = 0, because a vector cannot be perpendicular to itself in the required sense; the parallelogram it spans has no area.

🎯 EXAM TIP
Two facts get asked about directly. a × b = −(b × a) — the cross product is anticommutative, not commutative. And i × j = k, with the cycle i → j → k → i giving the positive results and the reverse direction giving negatives.
"}, "CALC3/ch1/s3": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Lines and planes are the flat building blocks of 3D geometry; tangent lines to curves and tangent planes to surfaces (coming later) are built exactly this way.

Line
A line through point P₀ = (x₀,y₀,z₀) with direction v = ⟨a,b,c⟩ has parametric equations x = x₀ + at, y = y₀ + bt, z = z₀ + ct.
Plane
A plane through P₀ with normal vector n = ⟨A,B,C⟩ satisfies n·(r − r₀) = 0, i.e. A(x−x₀) + B(y−y₀) + C(z−z₀) = 0.
WORKED EXAMPLE — plane through three points

Find the plane through P(1,0,0), Q(0,1,0), R(0,0,1).

Two edge vectors: PQ = ⟨−1,1,0⟩, PR = ⟨−1,0,1⟩. Normal n = PQ × PR = ⟨1, 1, 1⟩.

Plane: 1(x−1) + 1(y−0) + 1(z−0) = 0 ⇒ x + y + z = 1.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

The coefficients in a plane equation Ax + By + Cz = D are exactly the components of the normal vector ⟨A,B,C⟩. Read them off directly.

📊 FIGURE — A plane is a point plus a normal direction
Everything in the plane is perpendicular to the normal n = (a, b, c) — that single fact IS the equation a(x−x₀) + b(y−y₀) + c(z−z₀) = 0. Angles between planes are angles between normals; distance from a point is measured along n.
"}, "CALC3/ch2/s1": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Real quantities depend on many inputs at once (temperature on position, profit on price and quantity). A partial derivative measures the rate of change with respect to ONE variable while the others are held fixed — the foundation of all multivariable differentiation.

Partial derivative
For f(x,y), ∂f/∂x (also fx) is the ordinary derivative treating y as a constant; ∂f/∂y treats x as a constant.
WORKED EXAMPLE — computing partials

Let f(x,y) = x²y + 3y³. Find fx and fy.

fx: treat y as constant. d/dx(x²y) = 2xy; d/dx(3y³) = 0. So fx = 2xy.

fy: treat x as constant. d/dy(x²y) = x²; d/dy(3y³) = 9y². So fy = x² + 9y².

Second partials: fxx, fyy, and the mixed fxy. Clairaut's theorem: if the mixed partials are continuous, fxy = fyx.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

When taking ∂/∂x, every y is a frozen constant — so terms with only y differentiate to 0, and a y multiplying an x-term stays put.

📊 FIGURE — Partial derivatives are slopes of slices
Freeze y = b and the surface z = f(x, y) is cut into a single curve; its slope is ∂f/∂x. Freeze x instead for ∂f/∂y. A partial derivative is just an ordinary derivative taken along one slice of the surface.
"}, "CALC3/ch2/s2": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The gradient ∇f bundles all the partial derivatives into one vector that points in the direction of steepest increase — the key object behind directional derivatives, optimization, and gradient descent in machine learning.

Gradient
∇f = ⟨fx, fy, fz⟩. It points in the direction of maximum increase of f, and |∇f| is that maximum rate of change. ∇f is perpendicular to level curves/surfaces.
Chain rule
If z = f(x,y) with x = x(t), y = y(t), then dz/dt = fx·(dx/dt) + fy·(dy/dt) = ∇f · ⟨dx/dt, dy/dt⟩.
WORKED EXAMPLE — gradient at a point

For f(x,y) = x²+ y², find ∇f at (3, 4).

fx = 2x, fy = 2y, so ∇f = ⟨2x, 2y⟩. At (3,4): ∇f = ⟨6, 8⟩.

Direction of steepest ascent is ⟨6,8⟩; the maximum rate is |⟨6,8⟩| = 10.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

The gradient points uphill. Gradient descent (ML) moves in the negative gradient direction to minimize.

📊 FIGURE — The gradient is perpendicular to level curves
The ellipses are level curves of f (constant height, like a topographic map). At any point, ∇f points in the steepest uphill direction — always perpendicular to the level curve through that point. Walking ALONG a level curve changes nothing; walking WITH ∇f climbs fastest.
"}, "CALC3/ch2/s3": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

These are the payoff of partial derivatives: the directional derivative gives the slope in any direction, the tangent plane linearizes a surface, and setting ∇f = 0 finds maxima/minima — the core of optimization.

Directional derivative
In the direction of unit vector u, Duf = ∇f · u. It is maximized when u points along ∇f.
Tangent plane
The tangent plane to z = f(x,y) at (a,b) is z = f(a,b) + fx(a,b)(x−a) + fy(a,b)(y−b).
WORKED EXAMPLE — directional derivative

For f(x,y) = x² + y², find Duf at (1,2) in the direction of ⟨3,4⟩.

∇f = ⟨2x,2y⟩ = ⟨2,4⟩ at (1,2). Unit vector u = ⟨3,4⟩/5 = ⟨0.6, 0.8⟩.

Duf = ⟨2,4⟩·⟨0.6,0.8⟩ = 1.2 + 3.2 = 4.4.

Critical points: where ∇f = 0. Classify with the second-derivative test: D = fxxfyy − (fxy)². D>0 & fxx>0 → min; D>0 & fxx<0 → max; D<0 → saddle.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Always normalize the direction vector to a UNIT vector before dotting with ∇f — otherwise the directional derivative is scaled wrong.

📊 FIGURE — The gradient is perpendicular to level curves
The ellipses are level curves of f (constant height, like a topographic map). At any point, ∇f points in the steepest uphill direction — always perpendicular to the level curve through that point. Walking ALONG a level curve changes nothing; walking WITH ∇f climbs fastest.
📊 FIGURE — classifying a critical point
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Classifying (1, 1) for f = x³ − 3xy + y³

Find the critical point. f_x = 3x² − 3y and f_y = −3x + 3y². At (1, 1): f_x = 3 − 3 = 0 and f_y = −3 + 3 = 0, so it is critical.

Second derivatives. f_xx = 6x = 6, f_yy = 6y = 6, f_xy = −3.

Discriminant.

D = (6)(6) − (−3)² = 36 − 9 = 27 > 0

D > 0 with f_xx = 6 > 0, so (1, 1) is a local minimum.

For contrast, the same function's other critical point (0, 0) gives f_xx = 0, f_yy = 0, f_xy = −3, so D = 0 − 9 = −9 < 0 — a saddle.

🎯 EXAM TIP
Compute D = f_xx·f_yy − (f_xy)² first, because its sign decides the branch. Only when D > 0 do you look at f_xx to tell a minimum from a maximum. D < 0 is always a saddle, and D = 0 tells you nothing at all — the test has failed and you need another argument.
"}, "CALC3/ch3/s1": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

A single integral accumulates over an interval; a double integral ∬R f dA accumulates over a 2D region — giving volume under a surface, mass of a plate, and averages over areas.

Iterated integral
∬R f(x,y) dA = ∫cd ∫ab f(x,y) dx dy — integrate the inner variable first (treating the outer as constant), then the outer.
WORKED EXAMPLE — evaluating a double integral

Evaluate ∫₀¹ ∫₀² (x + y) dx dy.

Inner (in x, y constant): ∫₀² (x+y) dx = [x²/2 + yx]₀² = 2 + 2y.

Outer (in y): ∫₀¹ (2 + 2y) dy = [2y + y²]₀¹ = 2 + 1 = 3.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Match each limit to its variable. The inner differential's limits may depend on the outer variable, but the OUTER limits must be constants.

📊 FIGURE — A double integral adds tiny columns
Chop the region R into little cells of area dA; over each stands a column of height f(x, y). The double integral totals column volumes: ∬f dA. Iterated integrals compute it one direction at a time — inner integral first, then outer.
📊 FIGURE — swapping the order of integration
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Evaluating ∫₀² ∫₀¹ (x + 2y) dy dx

Work inside out. The inner integral is in y, so x is held constant:

∫₀¹ (x + 2y) dy = [xy + y²]₀¹ = x + 1

Then the outer integral in x:

∫₀² (x + 1) dx = [x²/2 + x]₀² = 2 + 2 = 4

Fubini says the other order must give the same answer. Checking: ∫₀¹ ∫₀² (x + 2y) dx dy = ∫₀¹ (2 + 4y) dy = 2 + 2 = 4. ✓

🎯 EXAM TIP
Fubini's theorem lets you swap the order of integration, with the limits correctly adjusted. Over a rectangle the limits are constants and swap unchanged; over a general region you must re-derive them from a sketch, and that re-derivation — not the integration — is where the marks are lost.
"}, "CALC3/ch3/s2": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Circular and radial regions are painful in x,y but natural in polar coordinates. The trick most people forget: dA = r dr dθ, not just dr dθ.

Polar double integral
∬R f dA = ∫∫ f(r cos θ, r sin θ) · r dr dθ. The extra factor r is the Jacobian of the polar transformation.
WORKED EXAMPLE — area of a circle via polar

Find the area of the disk r ≤ 2.

Area = ∫₀²π ∫₀² r dr dθ. Inner: ∫₀² r dr = [r²/2]₀² = 2. Outer: ∫₀²π 2 dθ = 4π.

Matches πr² = π(2²) = 4π ✓.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Forgetting the factor r is the #1 polar-integral error. dA = r dr dθ, always.

📊 FIGURE — Polar coordinates: (r, θ) instead of (x, y)
A point is located by its distance r from the origin and the angle θ from the positive x-axis. Conversion: x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, and r² = x² + y². The dashed circles are curves of constant r — the polar \"grid\".
📊 FIGURE — setting up in polar coordinates
🎯 EXAM TIP
The full disk of radius 3 at the origin is 0 ≤ r ≤ 3, 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π. The error that costs most marks in this section is not the limits though — it is forgetting that dA = r dr dθ. Omitting that factor of r silently produces the wrong answer for every polar integral.
"}, "CALC3/ch3/s3": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

A triple integral ∭ f dV accumulates over a solid region — volume, mass, and center of mass of 3D objects.

Triple integral
∭E f(x,y,z) dV is evaluated as three nested integrals; with f = 1 it gives the volume of E.
WORKED EXAMPLE — volume of a box

Find ∭ over the box 0≤x≤2, 0≤y≤3, 0≤z≤1 of the function 1.

∫₀¹∫₀³∫₀² 1 dx dy dz = ∫₀¹∫₀³ 2 dy dz = ∫₀¹ 6 dz = 6.

Matches length·width·height = 2·3·1 = 6 ✓.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Work from the inside out, and keep each variable's limits with its own integral sign. Sketch the solid if the limits depend on other variables.

📊 FIGURE — The volume element dV in three coordinate systems
Cartesian boxes: dV = dx dy dz. Cylindrical (polar + height): r dz dr dθ. Spherical: ρ² sin φ dρ dφ dθ. Choosing coordinates that match the solid’s symmetry is 90% of setting up a triple integral.
📊 FIGURE — the unit cube, done by symmetry
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — ∭ (x + y + z) dV over the unit cube

Split by linearity into three integrals. For the first:

∫₀¹∫₀¹∫₀¹ x dx dy dz = ∫₀¹∫₀¹ [x²/2]₀¹ dy dz = ∫₀¹∫₀¹ (1/2) dy dz = 1/2

The cube treats the three coordinates identically, so ∭ y dV and ∭ z dV are also 1/2 — no computation needed. Hence

∭ (x + y + z) dV = 1/2 + 1/2 + 1/2 = 3/2

Direct evaluation confirms 3/2. Spotting the symmetry turns three integrals into one.

🎯 EXAM TIP
Over a symmetric region, compute one term and reuse it. On the unit cube each coordinate integrates to 1/2, so ∭(x + y + z) dV = 3/2 immediately. Look for that symmetry before grinding out all three integrals.
"}, "CALC3/ch4/s1": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

A vector field assigns a vector to every point (wind velocity, electric field, fluid flow). Divergence measures net outflow (sources/sinks); curl measures rotation. These drive the fundamental theorems.

Divergence
For F = ⟨P, Q, R⟩, div F = ∇·F = ∂P/∂x + ∂Q/∂y + ∂R/∂z — a scalar. Positive divergence = a source.
Curl
curl F = ∇ × F, a vector measuring rotation. In 2D, the scalar curl of ⟨P,Q⟩ is ∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y.
WORKED EXAMPLE — divergence and curl

For F = ⟨x², y², z²⟩, div F = 2x + 2y + 2z.

For F = ⟨−y, x, 0⟩ (rotation), 2D scalar curl = ∂(x)/∂x − ∂(−y)/∂y = 1 − (−1) = 2 (constant rotation).

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Divergence eats a vector field and returns a SCALAR; curl returns a VECTOR. Don't swap them.

📊 FIGURE — Divergence vs. curl, visually
Left: a source — arrows flow outward, positive divergence (a sink points inward, negative). Right: rotation — arrows circulate, nonzero curl; a paddle wheel dropped here would spin. A field can have either, both, or neither.
📊 FIGURE — each component against its own variable
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — div⟨sin y, cos x, z⟩

Each component is differentiated only with respect to its matching variable:

  • P = sin y, so ∂P/∂x = 0 — there is no x in sin y
  • Q = cos x, so ∂Q/∂y = 0 — there is no y in cos x
  • R = z, so ∂R/∂z = 1

div F = 0 + 0 + 1 = 1

The trig functions are deliberately placed in the wrong slots. Anyone who differentiates sin y with respect to y gets cos y and a wrong answer — the pairing is fixed by position, not by which variable happens to appear.

🎯 EXAM TIP
For div F, the first component pairs with x, the second with y, the third with z — always. A question that puts sin y in the first slot is testing exactly that: the derivative is 0, not cos y. And the result is a scalar; if your answer is a vector you computed curl.
"}, "CALC3/ch4/s2": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

A line integral ∫C F·dr computes work done by a field along a path. For conservative fields, the work depends only on the endpoints — a huge shortcut.

Line integral (work)
∫C F·dr = ∫ab F(r(t))·r'(t) dt, where r(t) parametrizes the curve C.
Fundamental Theorem for line integrals
If F = ∇f, then ∫C F·dr = f(end) − f(start) — path-independent.
WORKED EXAMPLE — path-independent work

F = ∇f with f(x,y) = x²+ y². Find the work along ANY path from (0,0) to (1,2).

By the fundamental theorem: f(1,2) − f(0,0) = (1 + 4) − 0 = 5. The path doesn't matter.

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Path-independence only holds for CONSERVATIVE fields (curl F = 0). For a general field you must integrate along the specific path.

📊 FIGURE — A line integral totals the field’s push along the path
At each step dr along C, only the component of F pointing ALONG the path does work: F · dr. Adding these gives ∫_C F · dr. Where the field opposes the motion the contribution is negative — the integral nets it all out.
📊 FIGURE — two line-integral facts
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Why a closed loop gives zero, and what ∫1 ds measures

Closed loops. For a conservative field the line integral depends only on the endpoints: ∫_C F·dr = f(end) − f(start). On a closed loop the endpoint is the start point, so

∫_C F·dr = f(P) − f(P) = 0

This holds for any closed loop, which is exactly what \"conservative\" means physically: no net work is done going round and returning.

Arc length. Integrating the constant 1 with respect to arc length just totals the length of the curve. Along the straight segment from (0, 0) to (3, 4):

∫_C 1 ds = length = √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5

Note that this is a scalar line integral — no dot product and no direction. Reversing the direction of travel would flip the sign of ∫F·dr but leaves ∫1 ds unchanged.

🎯 EXAM TIP
For a conservative field, the circulation around any closed loop is zero — that is the defining property, and questions phrase it as \"work around a closed path\" or \"circulation\". Separately, ∫_C 1 ds is the arc length of C; here √(3² + 4²) = 5.
"}, "CALC3/ch4/s3": {"body": "
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

These three theorems each say the same profound thing: the integral of a derivative over a region equals a simpler integral over its boundary. They generalize the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus to 2D and 3D.

Green's theorem
∮C (P dx + Q dy) = ∬R (∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y) dA — a closed line integral in the plane equals a double integral of the scalar curl over the enclosed region.
Divergence theorem
∯S F·dS = ∭E div F dV — flux out through a closed surface equals the integral of divergence over the enclosed solid.
Stokes' theorem
∮C F·dr = ∬S (curl F)·dS — circulation around a boundary curve equals the flux of curl through any surface it bounds.
WORKED EXAMPLE — which theorem?

To convert a closed surface FLUX integral into a volume integral, use the Divergence theorem.

To convert a closed 2D line integral into a double integral, use Green's theorem (the 2D case of Stokes').

⚠ COMMON PITFALL

All three replace a boundary integral with a region integral of a derivative. Match by dimension: Green's = plane, Stokes' = surface in 3D, Divergence = solid in 3D.

📊 FIGURE — The grand pattern: boundary totals = interior totals
Green’s, Stokes’, and the divergence theorem all say one thing: adding a derivative-like quantity over the INSIDE equals measuring the field on the BOUNDARY. Interior micro-circulations cancel pairwise; only the outer rim survives.
"}, "CALC3/solving/sv1": {"body": "

Formulas & method

For f(x,y), the partial derivative ∂f/∂x treats y as a constant and differentiates in x (and vice-versa). The gradient is the vector of partials: ∇f = (∂f/∂x, ∂f/∂y). Evaluate at a point by substituting coordinates after differentiating.

Directional derivative

Along a unit vector u, D_u f = ∇f · u. Always normalize u first: if v = (a,b), then u = v/√(a²+b²).

Tangent plane / linear approximation

Near (a,b): z = f(a,b) + f_x(a,b)(x−a) + f_y(a,b)(y−b). Plug in the nearby point to estimate f.

Chain rule

If z = f(x,y) with x=x(t), y=y(t): dz/dt = (∂f/∂x)(dx/dt) + (∂f/∂y)(dy/dt).

Critical points

Solve f_x = 0 and f_y = 0 simultaneously; substitute back to get the value there. Use the Hessian D = f_xx·f_yy − (f_xy)² to classify: D>0 with f_xx>0 → local min.

Mini-example

f = x²y, ∂f/∂x = 2xy, ∂f/∂y = x². At (3,1): ∇f = (6, 9).

"}, "CALC3/solving/sv2": {"body": "

Formulas & method

A double integral over a rectangle is done as an iterated integral: ∫∫ f dA = ∫(∫ f dx) dy. Integrate the inner variable first, treating the other as constant, then integrate the result.

Divergence and curl

For F = (P, Q, R): div F = ∂P/∂x + ∂Q/∂y + ∂R/∂z (a scalar). curl F = (R_y − Q_z, P_z − R_x, Q_x − P_y) (a vector). Differentiate, then substitute the point.

Line integrals

For a conservative field F = ∇φ, ∫_C F·dr = φ(end) − φ(start), independent of path. E.g. F = (2x, 2y) has potential φ = x² + y².

Dot & cross product

a · b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃ (scalar). a × b = (a₂b₃−a₃b₂, a₃b₁−a₁b₃, a₁b₂−a₂b₁), with magnitude |a×b| = √(sum of squares) = |a||b|sinθ.

Mini-example

∫₀¹∫₀¹ xy dy dx: inner ∫₀¹ xy dy = x/2; then ∫₀¹ x/2 dx = 1/4.

"}, "CALC3/solving_only/sim": {"body": "

🧮 Solving Only

A practice set of only computational problems pulled from across this whole course — work out the answer and pick it from the options. Concept and definition questions are filtered out, so every item is something to solve. Reshuffled each time you start.

"}, "CALC3/solving2/sv1": {"body": "

Formulas & method

For a function f(x, y), the partial derivative ∂f/∂x is found by differentiating with respect to x while treating y as a constant; ∂f/∂y treats x as constant. Evaluate at a point by substituting the coordinates last.

Gradient

The gradient is the vector of first partials: ∇f = (∂f/∂x, ∂f/∂y). Its length is |∇f| = √((∂f/∂x)² + (∂f/∂y)²). The directional derivative in a unit direction u is the dot product D_u f = ∇f · u.

Chain rule

If z = f(x, y) with x = x(t) and y = y(t), then dz/dt = (∂f/∂x)(dx/dt) + (∂f/∂y)(dy/dt).

Critical points

A critical point occurs where both partials vanish: ∂f/∂x = 0 and ∂f/∂y = 0. Solve the system, then substitute back to get the function value.

Worked mini-example

Let f(x, y) = x²y + 3y². Then ∂f/∂x = 2xy and ∂f/∂y = x² + 6y. At the point (2, 1): ∂f/∂x = 2·2·1 = 4 and ∂f/∂y = 2² + 6·1 = 10. The gradient there is ∇f = (4, 10). Notice how the constant-during-differentiation variable simply rides along until the final substitution.

"}, "CALC3/solving2/sv2": {"body": "

Formulas & method

An iterated integral is evaluated from the inside out: integrate with respect to the inner variable first, holding the other constant, then integrate the result. For a rectangle, ∬ c dA = c · (area).

Divergence and curl

For F = (P, Q, R), the divergence is div F = ∂P/∂x + ∂Q/∂y + ∂R/∂z, a scalar. The curl is the vector curl F = (∂R/∂y − ∂Q/∂z, ∂P/∂z − ∂R/∂x, ∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y). Evaluate each expression, then substitute the point.

Line integrals

If F = ∇φ is conservative, then ∫_C F · dr = φ(end) − φ(start), independent of path. For F = (2x, 2y) the potential is φ = x² + y².

Vector products

The dot product a · b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃. The cross product a × b = (a₂b₃ − a₃b₂, a₃b₁ − a₁b₃, a₁b₂ − a₂b₁), with magnitude |a||b|sinθ.

Evaluate ∫₀¹ ∫₀¹ xy dx dy. The inner integral over x gives (y)·[x²/2]₀¹ = y/2. Then ∫₀¹ (y/2) dy = [y²/4]₀¹ = 1/4. Separable integrands factor into a product of single integrals, which speeds up such computations.

\n
THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its \"J-Method\"). Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. 📋 Vectors & the Geometry of Space

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Vectors, Length & the Dot Product

▸ Dot product For a = ⟨a₁,a₂,a₃⟩ and b = ⟨b₁,b₂,b₃⟩, the dot product is a·b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃ — a single number (scalar). Geometrically, a·b = |a||b|cos θ , where θ is the angle between them.

The Cross Product

▸ Cross product a × b = ⟨a₂b₃ − a₃b₂, a₃b₁ − a₁b₃, a₁b₂ − a₂b₁⟩. It is a vector , perpendicular to both a and b (right-hand rule). Its length |a × b| = |a||b|sin θ equals the area of the parallelogram they span.

Lines & Planes in Space

▸ Line A line through point P₀ = (x₀,y₀,z₀) with direction v = ⟨a,b,c⟩ has parametric equations x = x₀ + at, y = y₀ + bt, z = z₀ + ct.

▸ Plane A plane through P₀ with normal vector n = ⟨A,B,C⟩ satisfies n·(r − r₀) = 0 , i.e. A(x−x₀) + B(y−y₀) + C(z−z₀) = 0.

"}, "CALC3/cheat/c2": {"body": "

📋 Partial Derivatives

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Functions of Several Variables & Partial Derivatives

▸ Partial derivative For f(x,y), ∂f/∂x (also f x ) is the ordinary derivative treating y as a constant; ∂f/∂y treats x as a constant.

The Chain Rule & the Gradient

▸ Gradient ∇f = ⟨f x , f y , f z ⟩. It points in the direction of maximum increase of f, and |∇f| is that maximum rate of change. ∇f is perpendicular to level curves/surfaces.

▸ Chain rule If z = f(x,y) with x = x(t), y = y(t), then dz/dt = f x ·(dx/dt) + f y ·(dy/dt) = ∇f · ⟨dx/dt, dy/dt⟩.

Directional Derivatives, Tangent Planes & Optimization

▸ Directional derivative In the direction of unit vector u , D u f = ∇f · u . It is maximized when u points along ∇f.

▸ Tangent plane The tangent plane to z = f(x,y) at (a,b) is z = f(a,b) + f x (a,b)(x−a) + f y (a,b)(y−b).

"}, "CALC3/cheat/c3": {"body": "

📋 Multiple Integrals

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Double Integrals

▸ Iterated integral ∬ R f(x,y) dA = ∫ c d ∫ a b f(x,y) dx dy — integrate the inner variable first (treating the outer as constant), then the outer.

Double Integrals in Polar Coordinates

▸ Polar double integral ∬ R f dA = ∫∫ f(r cos θ, r sin θ) · r dr dθ. The extra factor r is the Jacobian of the polar transformation.

Triple Integrals

▸ Triple integral ∭ E f(x,y,z) dV is evaluated as three nested integrals; with f = 1 it gives the volume of E.

"}, "CALC3/cheat/c4": {"body": "

📋 Vector Calculus

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Vector Fields, Divergence & Curl

▸ Divergence For F = ⟨P, Q, R⟩, div F = ∇·F = ∂P/∂x + ∂Q/∂y + ∂R/∂z — a scalar. Positive divergence = a source.

▸ Curl curl F = ∇ × F, a vector measuring rotation. In 2D, the scalar curl of ⟨P,Q⟩ is ∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y.

Line Integrals & the Fundamental Theorem

▸ Line integral (work) ∫ C F·dr = ∫ a b F(r(t))·r'(t) dt, where r(t) parametrizes the curve C.

▸ Fundamental Theorem for line integrals If F = ∇f, then ∫ C F·dr = f(end) − f(start) — path-independent.

Green's, Stokes', and the Divergence Theorem

▸ Green's theorem ∮ C (P dx + Q dy) = ∬ R (∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y) dA — a closed line integral in the plane equals a double integral of the scalar curl over the enclosed region.

▸ Divergence theorem ∯ S F·dS = ∭ E div F dV — flux out through a closed surface equals the integral of divergence over the enclosed solid.

▸ Stokes' theorem ∮ C F·dr = ∬ S (curl F)·dS — circulation around a boundary curve equals the flux of curl through any surface it bounds.
